video.script:
G'day, and welcome to homestr8.

Deciding to take a hard look at your gambling takes guts, and you've already done the hardest part: you've started.

Here's how it works. Each morning, about ten minutes. A short video like this one, a guided audio, a quick check-in, and one small thing to try that day. Busy morning? There's a five-minute version.

There's no falling behind. Miss a day and the next session simply waits for you.

Two buttons are always there. Urge SOS, for when an urge hits. And Get help now, if you need a real person, any time of day or night.

Today is about one thing: why you're here. Let's find it.

audio.script:

Welcome. Before we talk about anything else, I want to say this: wanting to change your relationship with gambling doesn't make you weak, and it doesn't make you a bad person. Gambling is designed, very cleverly, to keep people coming back. Plenty of good, smart, hard-working people get caught up in it. What matters now is what you do next, and you're already doing it.

Today we're going to find your why. Your why is the reason you opened this app. It's the thing that will carry you through the tough days, so it's worth taking a few minutes to get it clear.

Let's start simply. Think about the moment you decided to download homestr8. What was going on? Maybe it was a big loss. Maybe it was a quiet feeling that's been building for a while. Maybe someone said something that stuck with you. There's no right answer. Just notice what comes up.

Now let's go a bit deeper. If gambling took up less of your life, or none of it, what would you get back?

Maybe it's money. Bills paid on time, a bit put away, no more checking your account with a knot in your stomach.

Maybe it's people. Being properly present with your partner, your kids, your mates. Not half there, with one eye on your phone.

Maybe it's your head. Sleeping through the night. Waking up without that heavy feeling. Not carrying a secret around.

Maybe it's trust, or pride, or just feeling in control of your own life again.

Take a moment and let one of those land. Which one matters most to you? You might find it's more than one, and that's fine too.

Now picture it. Really picture it. A normal day, some time from now, when gambling isn't calling the shots. Where are you? Who's with you? What are you doing with your Saturday? How does it feel to wake up that morning?

Stay with that picture for a few breaths.

That picture is your why. Hang on to it.

Here's the thing about your why: it isn't something you think about once. It's something you come back to, again and again, especially when an urge shows up. Urges are loud and they're in a hurry. Your why is quieter, but it's deeper. Over the next eight weeks you'll get better at hearing it over the noise.

A few things to know as you start.

You don't need to have everything worked out. You don't need to feel confident. You just need to keep showing up, one morning at a time.

If you slip up at some point, and many people do, it doesn't wipe out your progress. Every gamble-free day still counts. You dust yourself off and you pick up the next morning.

And you're not doing this on your own. If an urge hits, tap Urge SOS. If things ever feel like too much, tap Get help now, and you'll find people you can talk to straight away, any time.

Before we finish, let's put your why into words. Try finishing this sentence, out loud or in your head: "I'm doing this because..."

Say it once more, slowly. "I'm doing this because..."

Good. That's your anchor.

Take one last slow breath in... and out. When you're ready, head into your check-in. Well done for starting.

days.teaser: Tomorrow: How gambling hooks the brain.

video.script:
Ever wondered why gambling is so hard to walk away from? It's not because you're weak. It's because it's built that way.

Your brain has a reward system that lights up when something good might be about to happen. Not when it happens. When it might. That buzz of maybe is what gambling sells.

Wins come at random, which keeps your brain hooked far more than a steady reward would. Near misses feel like you nearly won, even though a miss is a miss. And the lights and sounds celebrate "wins" that are smaller than your bet.

Over time, the maths is set so the house comes out ahead.

Knowing how the hook works doesn't make you immune. But it does help you see it coming. That's today.

audio.title: How gambling hooks the brain
audio.script:
Get comfortable, and take a slow breath in... and out.

Yesterday you found your why. Today we're going to look at the other side of things: why gambling is so hard to step away from, even when part of you really wants to.

Let's start with something important. If you've ever thought, "What's wrong with me? Why can't I just stop?", I want you to hear this. Nothing is wrong with you. Gambling products are designed by very smart people, and tested on millions of others, to be as hard to put down as possible. You're up against a system that's built to keep you playing. Understanding that system is the first step to getting out of it.

So, how does it work?

Your brain has a reward system. It's there to help you survive. It nudges you towards things like food, connection and rest. When something good might be about to happen, your brain releases a chemical that creates a feeling of wanting, of anticipation. Notice that word: might. The strongest buzz often comes before the result, not after it. It's the moment the reels are spinning, the last few minutes of the game, the second before the result comes in.

That's the feeling gambling sells. Not the win itself, but the maybe.

Now, here's the clever part. If you won every time, or never won at all, your brain would soon lose interest. But gambling pays out at random. Sometimes you win, often you don't, and you never know which it'll be. Scientists have found that random rewards like this are one of the most powerful ways to keep any creature coming back. It's the same reason it's hard to stop checking your phone.

There are a few other tricks layered on top.

Near misses. When you almost win, two symbols out of three, the team losing by a point, your brain reacts a lot like it does to a win. It tells you that you were close, that next time could be it. But a near miss is just a loss. You weren't any closer.

Losses dressed up as wins. On many machines, the lights flash and the music plays when you "win" back less than you put in. You've lost money, but it feels like a win.

Chasing. After a loss, there's a strong pull to win it back. It can feel like the only way to fix things. But chasing usually makes the hole deeper, because the maths doesn't change just because you're behind.

And underneath all of it, the maths. Every product is set up so that over time, the house comes out ahead. Some people win some of the time. But the longer anyone plays, the more the numbers favour the house. That isn't bad luck. It's the business model.

Take a breath here. That's a lot.

So what do you do with all this?

First, go easy on yourself. Getting hooked by something that's designed to hook people isn't a personal failing.

Second, start noticing. Over the next few days, if you feel the pull, see if you can name what's happening. "That's the maybe feeling." "That's my brain chasing." "That was a near miss, which is just a miss." Naming it puts a bit of space between you and the urge. And space is where your choices live.

Third, remember that urges pass. That buzz of anticipation rises, peaks and fades, usually within about half an hour, whether you act on it or not. You don't have to fight it. You just have to wait it out. That's what Urge SOS is for.

You'll learn much more about the tricks in Bookie Tricks Exposed, in the Explore tab, whenever you've got a few spare minutes.

Let's finish with a slow breath in... and out.

You now know more about how the hook works than most people ever will. That's real power. Head into your check-in when you're ready.

video.script:
Let's talk about money. Not to make you feel bad. To help you take back control of it.

When you're caught up in gambling, it's easy to stop looking. The bank balance becomes something you avoid. But money you don't look at is money that slips away.

Today's reflection is a gentle, honest look. Roughly what has gambling been costing you? And, more importantly, what would you rather that money did for you?

A holiday. A car that doesn't break down. Getting on top of a debt. A bit put away for a rainy day. Something special for the kids.

Your goal isn't a punishment. It's something to move towards. Let's find yours.

audio.title: Your money, your goal
audio.script:
Settle in, and take a slow breath in... and out.

Today's a reflection, so there's nothing to learn and nothing to get right. Just a few questions to sit with, in your own time.

We're going to talk about money. For a lot of people, this is the hardest part. There can be guilt, or shame, or a sinking feeling just thinking about it. If that's you, that's completely understandable. Notice that feeling, and let it be there. We're not here to add up everything that's gone wrong. We're here to look forward.

Let's start gently. Without working out exact numbers, just roughly: in a usual week, how much has been going on gambling? It doesn't have to be precise. A rough idea is plenty.

Now let's stretch that out a little. Think about a month. Then think about a year. You don't need to do the maths perfectly. Just let the size of it land.

How does that feel? Some people feel a jolt. Some people feel sad. Some people feel relief, because it's finally out in the open. Whatever you feel is okay. Breathe with it for a moment.

Now here's the part I really want you to focus on. That money isn't gone forever. From today, every gamble-free day keeps some of it with you. So the question becomes: what would you rather that money did?

Let's imagine a few possibilities. See which one gives you a little lift.

Maybe it's a trip. A week somewhere warm, or a road trip with the family, paid for in full.

Maybe it's getting out from under something. Paying off a credit card, or a loan, and feeling that weight come off.

Maybe it's something for the people you love. Footy fees, a new bike for the kids, a proper dinner out with your partner.

Maybe it's something for you. A gym setup, tools for the shed, a decent car.

Or maybe it's just breathing room. Money in the bank, so the next unexpected bill isn't a crisis.

Pick one. If more than one comes up, pick the one that makes you smile, or the one that would make the biggest difference.

Now picture having it. Picture the moment it's yours, or the moment that debt is gone. Where are you? Who are you telling? How does it feel?

Stay with that for a few breaths.

That's your goal. And here's how it connects to everything else. Every time you ride out an urge, every gamble-free day, you're moving towards that picture. Not in some vague way. In actual dollars.

In the app, you can set this goal, or change the one you picked when you started. Tap the Money kept card on Home, or go to More, then Your goal. You'll be able to watch it fill up.

One more thought before we finish. Some people find it helps to make their money a bit harder to get to in a weak moment. Things like paying bills and moving savings first thing on payday, or asking your bank to block gambling payments on your card. We'll talk more about that soon.

Let's close with a slow breath in... and out.

Your money is yours again, starting today. Head into your check-in when you're ready.

Every gamble-free day, you keep money that would have gone. The app counts it for you, using what you told us you usually spend. It's an estimate, but it's your money, and watching it grow helps.

Not everything you keep is money, though. Time. Sleep. Patience with the kids. Not checking your phone every five minutes. Those count too.

Today we'll also make the money harder to get to in a weak moment. Your bank can usually block gambling payments on your card. If you've chosen to stop completely, BetStop can block every licensed online betting company in Australia with one sign-up. It's free.

audio.title: Counting what you keep
audio.script:
Get comfortable, and breathe in... and out.

Yesterday you thought about where you'd like your money to go. Today is about two things: noticing what you're keeping, and making it easier to keep it.

Let's start with keeping count.

On your Home screen there's a card called Money kept. Every gamble-free day, it goes up by a day's worth of what you told us you usually spend. It's an estimate, not your bank balance, but it's a fair picture of the money that's staying with you instead of going out the door. When things get tough, it can really help to see that number.

But here's something that often surprises people. The money is only part of it. When gambling takes up less of your life, you tend to get other things back too, and they're easy to miss if you're not looking.

Let's look now. Think back over the last day or two. Have you noticed anything at all? Maybe a bit more time in the evening. Maybe you went to bed earlier. Maybe you weren't checking scores or results all through dinner. Maybe you felt a little lighter, or a little prouder of yourself.

It might be small. That's fine. Small things are exactly what we're looking for. Each day in your check-in, see if you can notice one thing you kept that wasn't money.

Take a breath.

Now the second part: making it easier.

Here's an honest truth. Willpower is useful, but it runs out. It runs out when you're tired, stressed, bored, a few drinks in, or when the footy's on and everyone's betting. So rather than relying on willpower alone, it makes sense to put a few barriers between you and gambling. That way, when the urge hits, there's time for it to pass before you can act on it.

Here are some barriers people find helpful. See which ones fit you.

Your bank. Most of the big Australian banks let you block gambling payments on your card, usually in the banking app under card settings. If you're not sure how, you can call your bank and ask.

Betting apps and accounts. Deleting the apps, closing accounts and unsubscribing from their emails and texts. Out of sight really does help.

BetStop. If you've decided to stop completely, BetStop is a free government register. One sign-up blocks you from every licensed online and phone betting company in Australia, for anywhere from three months to life. In the app you'll find it under More. It doesn't cover pokies or casinos, but for those, venues have their own self-exclusion programs, and Gambling Help Online can help you find them.

Blocking apps. There are apps that stop betting sites opening on your phone and computer.

And cash. Some people find it helps to carry less cash, or to have their pay go straight into an account that's harder to get to.

You don't have to do all of these. Pick one that feels doable today. Just one.

Notice if part of you is resisting. If a little voice says, "But what if I want a bet later?", that's normal. That voice is the hook we talked about on Day 2. You don't have to argue with it. Just notice it, and do the thing anyway.

Let's finish with a breath in... and out.

Every barrier you put up is a gift to the version of you who's having a tough moment. Head into your check-in when you're ready.

days.teaser: Tomorrow: The people in your corner.

video.script:
Gambling loves secrecy. It grows when you're carrying it on your own.

That's why today is about the people in your corner. Not everyone needs to know. But having even one person you can be honest with can make a big difference.

It might be a partner, a mate, a brother or sister, a parent. Someone who'll listen without lecturing.

In the app you can add a buddy. Each week they'll get a short email saying how many sessions you've done, with an idea for how to back you up. It never mentions gambling or money.

And there's always someone ready to talk. Gambling Help Online is free, confidential and open 24/7 on 1800 858 858. Talking to people who've been there, through groups like Gamblers Anonymous or SMART Recovery, helps a lot of people too.

Who's in your corner?

audio.title: The people in your corner
audio.script:
Get comfortable, and take a slow breath in... and out.

Today we're going to talk about people. Because one of the things gambling does, quietly, is make people feel alone.

It's very common to keep gambling hidden. Some people hide how much they spend. Some hide how often. Some hide it altogether. Usually it's not because they're dishonest people. It's because of shame, or not wanting to worry anyone, or fear of what might happen if it came out.

The trouble is, secrecy is where gambling does best. When it's hidden, there's no one to notice when things are getting worse, no one to talk to when an urge hits, and a lot of energy goes into keeping the secret.

So today, let's think about who's in your corner. Not who you think should be. Who actually is.

Let's do a little exercise. Picture a few circles, one inside the other, with you in the middle.

In the closest circle, think of the one or two people you trust most. People who've got your back. They don't have to be perfect. They just have to care about you.

In the next circle, people you get on with and could talk to if you needed. Mates, workmates, family members, someone from the footy club or the gym.

And in the outer circle, people whose job it is to help, and who've heard it all before. Counsellors. Your GP. The team at Gambling Help Online.

Take a moment to fill in those circles in your mind. Who comes up?

If your circles feel a bit empty right now, that's okay. Lots of people feel that way, especially when gambling has pulled them away from people. That outer circle is always there, and it's a good place to start.

Now, here's a question to sit with. Is there one person who you could tell, even a little, about what you're doing with this app?

You don't have to tell them everything. You could start small. Something like, "I'm trying to cut back on something that's been getting out of hand, and I'm doing a program in the mornings." Or, "I'm having a go at giving up the betting. Could you check in on me now and then?"

Notice how it feels to imagine saying that. A bit scary? A bit of relief? Both are normal.

If you'd like some backup, the app has a buddy feature. You can add someone's email, with their okay, and each week they'll get a short, kind email saying how many sessions you've done, with an idea for how to support you. It never mentions gambling or money, so it's discreet. You'll find it in Settings, under Your buddy.

And remember the people whose whole job is to help. Gambling Help Online is free, confidential and open all day, every day, on 1800 858 858, or by online chat. You don't have to be in crisis to call. You can call just to talk things through. There are also peer support groups, like Gamblers Anonymous and SMART Recovery, where you can meet people who understand from the inside.

Let's finish with something kind. Picture someone who cares about you hearing that you're doing this program. Picture their face. Most people, when someone they love says, "I'm working on something hard," feel proud of them, not disappointed.

Take a breath in... and out.

You don't have to do this alone. Head into your check-in when you're ready.

video.script:
Big changes are made of small steps. Not one heroic decision, but lots of ordinary ones. A morning session. An urge you let pass. A night you went to bed instead of scrolling.

None of them feel like much on their own. Together, they change things.

Today's session is a guided meditation. It's a chance to slow down, notice your breathing, and practise something that's really useful when an urge turns up: letting a feeling be there without having to act on it.

If you've never done a meditation before, that's fine. There's nothing to get right. If your mind wanders, that's normal. Just come back.

Find a quiet spot, and let's begin.

audio.title: Small steps add up
audio.script:
Find a comfortable position, sitting or lying down. If it feels okay, let your eyes close, or just let your gaze rest on the floor in front of you.

Take a slow breath in through your nose... and let it out through your mouth.

And again. In... and out.

Now let your breathing find its own rhythm. You don't need to control it. Just notice it. The air coming in, cool. The air going out, a little warmer.

Let's start by noticing your body. Feel where you're touching the chair, or the bed, or the floor. Let it hold your weight. You don't have to hold yourself up right now.

Notice your feet. Your legs. Let them be heavy.

Notice your stomach, rising and falling with each breath.

Notice your shoulders. If they've crept up towards your ears, let them drop.

Notice your jaw. Let it soften.

Good. Just breathing.

At some point, your mind will wander. It might go to something you need to do today, or something that's worrying you. That's completely normal. Minds wander. When you notice it's wandered, that noticing is the skill. Gently bring your attention back to your breath. No telling yourself off. Just come back.

Now let's think about this week. You've been showing up. Maybe every morning, maybe not. Either way, you're here now, and that counts.

Picture a path. Not a steep mountain. Just an ordinary walking track, winding off into the distance. You're on it. Each step on its own is small. You can't see the end from here, and you don't need to. You only need to take the next step.

Breathe in... and out.

Now let's practise something you can use any time. Bring to mind a mild feeling of wanting. It doesn't have to be about gambling. It might be wanting a coffee, or wanting to check your phone. Just something small.

Notice where you feel it in your body. Maybe a pull in your chest. A restlessness in your hands. A tightness somewhere.

Now, instead of doing anything about it, just watch it. Like you're watching a wave at the beach. It rises... it peaks... and if you don't feed it, it starts to settle.

You don't have to fight it. You don't have to obey it. You can just let it be there, and let it pass.

That's what you'll do with gambling urges too. It's called urge surfing. You ride the wave instead of being knocked over by it. And every time you do it, you get a bit better at it.

Breathe in... and out.

Before we finish, let's offer yourself something kind. Many people are very hard on themselves. If you are, try saying this, quietly, in your head: "I'm doing my best. That's enough for today."

One more time. "I'm doing my best. That's enough for today."

Now start to bring your attention back to the room. Notice the sounds around you. Wriggle your fingers and toes. Take a deeper breath.

When you're ready, open your eyes.

Small steps add up. You took one today. Head into your check-in when you're ready.

For many people, gambling has a rhythm. It shows up at the same times each week, almost like an appointment. And because it's so regular, it can stop feeling like a choice. It just becomes what happens at that time.

Let's map out your week. Picture a normal week, starting on Monday.

Monday morning. Back to work, or back to the routine. Is there any pull here? For some people, Monday is fine. For others, it's when the weekend's losses sink in.

Now the weekend. Saturday, when the sport is on. Sunday afternoon, which can feel long and empty.

And then there are the times that don't come every week. Payday, if it's fortnightly or monthly. Grand finals and other big sporting events. Holidays. Birthdays. Christmas. Times when you've got a bit of extra money, or a lot of extra time.

Take a moment and pick out your top two or three risky times. When does the urge show up most?

If late at night is risky, could you put your phone on charge outside the bedroom, and read, or just go to sleep earlier?

If payday is risky, we'll talk about that on Day 13. It's a big one.

video.script:
A lot of gambling isn't really about money. It's about feelings.

Stress after a hard day. Boredom on a long Sunday. Loneliness late at night. Feeling flat, or anxious, or angry. Even feeling good, like wanting to celebrate.

For a while, gambling can take the edge off. It gives you something to focus on. It switches off the noise. But the relief doesn't last, and the losses usually leave you feeling worse than before.

Today we'll look at the feelings that pull you in. And we'll find other ways to deal with them. Ways that actually help, and don't cost you.

It starts with noticing what you're really feeling.

audio.title: Feelings that pull you in
audio.script:
Get comfortable, and take a slow breath in... and out.

Today we're looking at one of the most powerful triggers of all: feelings.

When people think about gambling, they often think it's about money. Trying to win. But for a lot of people, if they're really honest, it's more about what gambling does to how they feel. It can be a way of escaping. Switching off. Getting a buzz when life feels flat. Having something to look forward to.

Let's go through some of the most common feelings, and see which ones you recognise.

Stress. After a hard day at work, or when money's tight, or when there's tension at home. Gambling can feel like a break from all of it.

Boredom. Long weekends. Quiet nights. Times when there's nothing much to do. Gambling fills the space and makes time go faster.

Loneliness. When you're on your own, especially at night. Gambling can feel like company.

Feeling low, or flat. When nothing feels very good. The buzz of maybe can feel like the only thing that lights you up.

Anger or frustration. After an argument, or a bad day. Gambling can feel like letting off steam.

And sometimes, good feelings too. Celebrating. Feeling lucky. Having a bit of extra cash. Wanting to keep a good feeling going.

Take a moment. Which of these do you recognise? There might be one big one, or a few.

Here's the thing to understand. Gambling does work, a little bit, in the moment. That's why it's so easy to reach for. It does give you a break from the feeling. But it's a bit like using a credit card to pay off another credit card. The relief doesn't last, and the cost comes later. Losses lead to more stress, more low moods, more secrecy, and the cycle goes round again.

So the question isn't how to stop having these feelings. Everyone has them. The question is: what else could you do with them?

Let's go through a few ideas.

For stress: move your body. A walk, a run, a swim, the gym. Even ten minutes. Or Urge SOS, and three minutes of slow breathing. Stress lives in the body, and the body is the quickest way to shift it.

For boredom: have a list ready. Things you can do when you've got time on your hands. A job around the house. A project in the shed. Cooking something. Calling someone. Getting out of the house. Boredom is much harder to deal with if you're trying to think of something on the spot.

For loneliness: reach out. A text to a mate, a call to family, even just going somewhere where there are people, like the gym or the local footy. And remember, Gambling Help Online is there 24/7, if you need someone to talk to.

For feeling low: be kind to yourself, and look after the basics. Sleep, food, getting outside. And if low moods are hanging around for weeks, it's worth talking to your GP. Feeling low and gambling often go together, and getting help with one can really help with the other.

For anger: give it somewhere to go. A hard workout. A walk to cool off. Writing it down.

For celebrating: find another way to mark it. A good meal. Time with people you like. Putting something towards your goal.

Before we finish, try something. Next time you feel an urge, pause, and ask yourself: what am I actually feeling right now? Just name it. "I'm stressed." "I'm bored." "I'm lonely." Naming a feeling often takes a bit of the heat out of it, and it points you towards what you actually need.

Breathe in... and out.

Your feelings make sense. You just deserve better ways of looking after them. Head into your check-in when you're ready.

Today we're looking at the people side of triggers. Because for a lot of people, gambling isn't something they do alone. It's woven into their social life.

Let's think about where that happens for you.

Maybe it's mates who bet on the footy, and the group chat that lights up every game day. Maybe it's a work sweep, or workmates who go to the pub on Fridays. Maybe it's a family that always has a bet at Christmas, or a club where everyone ends up in the gaming room. Maybe it's one particular mate who you always seem to end up gambling with.

Take a moment, and notice who comes to mind. There's no blame in this. These might be people you love. We're just noticing where the pressure comes from.

Now let's think about the other side. Who in your life makes it easier not to gamble? People you do other things with. People who don't bet, or who wouldn't care if you didn't. Notice who comes up there too.

Here's the thing about social pressure. Most of it isn't people actually pushing you. It's the feeling of being left out, or the worry about what people will think. And that worry is usually a lot bigger in our heads than it is in real life.

So let's get you ready. When someone says, "You in?" or "Put twenty on for me," what will you say?

The best answers are short, honest enough, and said like it's no big deal. You don't owe anyone a long explanation. Here are a few you could try. See which one feels like you.

"Nah, I'm right, mate."

"I'm having a break from it."

"I'm saving for something."

"Not for me at the moment."

"I'm giving the betting a rest."

Pick one. Say it to yourself now, a couple of times, the way you'd say it to a mate.

It might feel a bit strange at first. That's normal. The first few times are the hardest. After that, most people find their mates just stop asking.

Now let's think about some practical things.

If there's a group chat that's all about betting, could you mute it on game days? Or leave it, and stay in touch with those mates in other ways?

If your Friday drinks always end up at the pokies, could you head off before that happens? Or suggest somewhere else?

If there's one person you always end up gambling with, could you see them for something else? A game of golf, a feed, a fishing trip?

And if there's someone you trust, it can really help to tell them what you're doing. Not everyone, just one or two people. When your mates know, they're often happy to back you up, and they'll stop asking.

You might find some people react in a way you don't expect. Most will be fine, and some will be really supportive. If someone gives you a hard time about it, that tells you something about them, not about you.
